A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study by Redhardt, Akram and Schug. The main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite the revised title and rearranged appendix material.

before.justification: Sections 3–4 and Appendix B report original scaling, constituent-decoding and image-generation experiments on synthetic task families and four image-generation models.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, with additional model-size results in Figure 1 and a deep-hyperteacher experiment in Appendix B.3.

M1.justification: The MLP and transformer learners, task encodings, training objectives and constituent-decoding procedures are retained. The deeper hyperteacher is an added configuration of the experimental task generator, not a revised learning method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate hyperteacher regression, compositional preference-grid tasks and the same 27 image-composition task families. The deeper teacher varies the configuration of the retained synthetic task family without introducing a new domain or task requirement.

E2.justification: The MLP-versus-transformer comparison is retained in v1 Figure 8 and v2 Figure 10. The image-model comparison still includes FLUX.1-dev, SD XL base 1.0, SD 3.0 medium and SD 3.5 medium.

E3.justification: Appendix B.3 adds a data-scaling evaluation using a hyperteacher task network with three hidden layers of 16 neurons each, alongside the original single-hidden-layer experiments. Existing evaluation metrics, training-support procedures and selected hyperparameters in Table 3 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figure 11 tests whether the scaling finding survives increased task-network depth. Figure 1 also adds model-size sensitivity curves at several held-out task fractions. Existing encoding, training-support and constituent-decodability analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The retained experiments continue to report SEM over three seeds and ordinary-least-squares R² values with corresponding p-values. No revised run counts, seed policy or uncertainty-estimation procedure is disclosed.

E6.justification: Figure 1 adds model-size results for held-out fractions from 0.99 to 0.999. New Figure 11 reports that deeper hyperteacher tasks are harder but still exhibit improving compositional generalization with data scale. Tables 1–2 and the matched original scaling, decoding and image-generation plots retain their results.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 replaces O(M/epsilon²) with O(M + epsilon^(-1/2)), introducing explicit uniformly bounded weights, compact inputs and a constituent domain satisfying ||z||_1 <= 1. Appendix A.2 adds Lemma A.4 and a fixed-depth multilayer extension, Theorem A.5, with an induction proof. Lemma A.2 also changes non-equivalently: its subtracted slope term now uses ReLU(x - x_{i-1}), causing cancellation rather than the claimed interpolation.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and discussion retain the same central claims: scaling can enable compositional generalization given adequate task coverage, MLP expressivity scales linearly with module count, and constituent decodability tracks compositional success. The qualified title and additional evidence do not materially redefine these already conditional claims.

C2.justification: Section 6 newly distinguishes existence of a compact generalizing solution from guarantees that SGD will discover it, explicitly identifying the latter as an open question and discussing simplicity bias. The existing limitations concerning ambiguous task specifications and unknown real-world generative processes remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 specifies the added teacher configuration as three hidden layers with 16 neurons each. Existing implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware, compute estimates, software dependencies and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: Nine references are added, expanding the historical connectionism discussion and coverage of modular networks, hierarchical compositional learning, language-model function composition and optimization bias. All earlier references remain, and the central positioning relative to architectural approaches is unchanged.

P1.justification: The title becomes 'Scaling can lead to compositional generalization'; author information and publication headers are updated. Proof exposition and limitations expand, and Appendix B places preference-grid results before transformers. Most main-text wording and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned with a model-size panel and fewer displayed held-out fractions. Figure 4 explicitly distinguishes training and evaluation tiles, and a new deep-hyperteacher Figure 11 is added. Figure 3 and appendix figures/tables are relocated or regrouped; most existing graphics and table structures are retained.

improvement.justification: The added depth experiment and explicit SGD limitation improve empirical support and interpretation, while the revised theorem makes its assumptions clearer and adds a multilayer extension. However, unlike v1, the interpolation formula in Lemma A.2 cancels interior contributions and fails its stated interpolation property. This introduces a proof defect into the construction supporting the revised theoretical results. With useful empirical and explanatory gains but impaired mathematical presentation in the largest substantive revision, the net quality direction is unclear.
